## Findings by module

### 1

- **refined** (ch-015.txt): GHA IX (Konate) gives the original publication years as I and II 1981, III 1988, IV 1984, V 1992, VI 1989, VII 1985 and VIII 1995 (elsewhere in the same volume 1987 for VII and 1993 for VIII), so the series' own dates are inconsistent: state 1985 or 1987 for VII and 1993 for VIII and say the volume disagrees with itself [CONTESTED]
- **extended** (ch-017.txt): GHA IX (Rajaonah, 2024) dates volume VII: it dates its publication to 1987, its latest references to 1981 and its contributions to the 1970s (chapters 8 and 15 written in 1976 and 1974), so it carries the post-independence concern with resistance and nationalism. The copy we hold is cited as 1985 in the course refs; give both dates and note the review's
- **extended** (ch-015.txt): GHA IX (Konate): the series was a post-independence project (Ki-Zerbo: history is a source of development like mines and plantations; Mbow's preface rejects the Hegelian denial of African history); the 1970s-80s 'nationalist history' celebrated great African figures; Volume IX's guidance memo says it aims to update earlier volumes for new research and politics. Reviewers find the series solid but some chapters could not be reproduced unchanged; Coquery-Vidrovitch says Ajayi's volume VI opening chapter could be published almost unchanged
- **extended** (ch-004.txt): GHA IX (Holl) frames the series as a corrective to the 'colonial library'; says the eight volumes were published 1981 to 1999 (and in another sentence that volume VIII 'was already dated just a few years after its publication in 1990', yet front matter says 1993), so the date of volume VIII varies across the volume: 1990, 1993, 1995, 1999. Volumes I and II most need updating; VIII was already dated soon after publication
- **note** (ch-017.txt): GHA IX on volume VII's limits: only one woman among its authors (Coquery-Vidrovitch), almost no treatment of education or gender; about one million African subjects enlisted in WWI (Ndiaye: 300,000 Black people from Africa and America reached France); colonial rule was negotiated on the ground, not only imposed (Cooper and Stoler)
- **note** (ch-004.txt): GHA IX (Holl): research agendas on Africa were set by Euro-American institutions; African scholars outside the Western mainstream are silenced by gatekeeping and non-citation (Karega-Munene and Schmidt); the volume's own aim is a selective update, not a replacement of volumes I-VIII, and its concept of 'global Africanity' is contested
- **note** (ch-005.txt): GHA IX (Yai, Ze Belinga): the first eight volumes had almost no epistemological reflection (the word appears three times in volume I; one of twelve 'studies and documents' issues); reservations remain about their chronological and geographical coverage of resistance and a persisting Eurocentric narrative, with categories such as Middle Ages, feudalism and uniform slavery still common. A critical review of volumes I-VIII was done under Konate (2009)

### 2

- **refined** (ch-017.txt): GHA IX: the volume's view that resistance led on to nationalism is now debated (Ranger's primary and secondary resistance; a shift from collaboration versus resistance to 'alternative strategies'); resistance can be passive and is not only a defence of an old order. Conquest violence ended in genocide for some societies (Reid, Davis); the 1890s were among the worst decades (drought, famine, epizootics, epidemics). Use as a caveat on the Module 2 resistance cases
- **extended** (ch-015.txt): GHA IX (Konate) on volume VII: the resistant-versus-collaborating dichotomy is simplistic; reactions ranged from armed resistance to alliance, accommodation and non-collaboration; Ethiopia and Liberia were nominally independent but under economic influence of the powers; religion and art were spaces of relative freedom under colonial rule

### 3

- **refined** (ch-017.txt): GHA IX: pan-Africanism is conventionally dated to the London conference of 1900, but Olisanwuche dates it to 1893 (Chicago) with Atlanta in 1895 and Henry Sylvester Williams's African Association in 1897; volume VII reviews the first conference and first three congresses, all in European capitals, and treats diaspora links in about forty pages. Also: SANNC founded at Bloemfontein 1912 by Seme and Plaatje, becoming the ANC 'around ten years later'
- **contradicted** (ch-003.txt): GHA IX (Holl) says the Sirte Declaration of 09/09/1999 was the founding act of the OAU, which became the African Union in 2002; the OAU Charter was signed on 25/05/1963 (see our OAU Charter source), and Sirte launched the process that created the AU. Do not repeat the GHA IX wording; teach it as a slip in a secondary source [FIRM correction]
- **extended** (ch-018.txt): GHA IX (Barbosa): volume VIII's pan-Africanism chapters lack data on women and communist organisations in the movement, now better studied (Adi on pan-Africanism and communism); Mazrui treats 1935, the invasion of Ethiopia, as Africa's start of the Second World War; the 1975 Cotonou minutes asked for a 'more African rather than a purely postcolonial' viewpoint; Barbosa praises its balanced view of nation-building 1960-80 as a strength
- **extended** (ch-015.txt): GHA IX (Konate) on volume VIII: Section VI treats pan-Africanism and the diasporas with a 'foundational' role for the diaspora; the review stresses the need for dialogue between Africans and the diasporas; absence of women's business roles is noted by all reviews; Volume IX's key concept is 'global Africanity', which the review calls much-debated
- **extended** (ch-003.txt): GHA IX (Holl): the GHA was launched by UNESCO in 1964, about 350 historians (two thirds African), an International Scientific Committee of 39; published 1981 to 1999; hardly used in African school curricula, which led to the Pedagogical Use project (Tripoli 06/2010, funded by Libya, later without funding after the destruction in Libya). Pan-Africanism was coined and nurtured by diaspora intellectuals mostly in the nineteenth century; the OAU and AU are its clearest political form
- **note** (ch-007.txt): GHA IX (Somet) traces the 'colonial library' to Enlightenment race writing (Hume 1753, Kant 1764, Hegel's lectures) and 'scientific' racism (Morton, Nott and Gliddon), and credits Anténor Firmin's 1885 reply; but it also asserts that ancient Egypt was 'a country of Negroes' and that the Black race preceded all others, a claim Holl's own introduction in the same volume states differently (Egypt is African with a fluctuating mix of African and Eurasian populations, and the 'ownership' question is not the point). Use as background for the Module 3 Lynch lesson only with that caveat [CONTESTED]

### 4

- **contradicted** (ch-003.txt): GHA IX (Holl) gives Guinea-Bissau and Cabo Verde independence on 24/09/1973, Angola 11/11/1974 and Mozambique 25/06/1975; GHA VIII's Table 5.1 gives Guinea-Bissau 10/09/1974, Cabo Verde 05/07/1975 and Angola 11/11/1975, which the course should follow. Guinea-Bissau declared independence on 24/09/1973 (recognised 1974), but Cabo Verde and Angola are wrong in GHA IX. Namibia 21/03/1990, Mandela freed 11/02/1990 and Lumumba killed 17/01/1961 in GHA IX match the course
- **extended** (ch-018.txt): GHA IX (Barbosa) dates volume VIII: it was written and published in 1993, covers 1935 to 1992 (afterword by Wondji up to 1997), and its omissions are listed: Thomas Sankara's 1983-87 revolution (contemporary with publication), gender (one woman author among 43), African diasporas (only chapters 23-24, US-focused), rural Africa, health and disease, sexuality, children and youth; coverage of 1935-60 is thin (92 pages for 1935-45, 210 for 1945 to independence, most countries 2-3 pages)
- **note** (ch-018.txt): Reading note: the last page of Barbosa's review (about 650 words, from the Cotonou minutes to the references) fell into the next block after the cut and was read directly from the file, not through the reader; it adds no new figures: Nkrumah's call for one African government compared to Bolivar's dream, and the point that the internal-external dialectic remains valid

### 7

- **note** (ch-003.txt): GHA IX (Holl) context for Module 7: African growth averaged about 5 per cent a year in recent years; Africa's share of world trade is a marginal 2 per cent; the African Continental Free Trade Area agreement was signed in Kigali on 21/03/2018 by 44 states (the course has trading from 01/01/2021); Volume IX frames 'Global Africa', Brazil's law on teaching African history funded it, and the volume names structural adjustment as disastrous for most African countries
